Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Authority Presence: Police, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

Vignette:
Dr. Nguyen's eyes scanned the crowded hospital corridor, her gaze lingering on each stranger's face before quickly moving on, searching for a familiar feature, a spark of recognition that would send her heart racing. It had been two years since the assault, but the memory still felt like an open wound, festering and tender to the touch. That night was etched in her mind like a scar - the sound of footsteps behind her, the feeling of hands grasping at her clothes, the smell of sweat and fear that clung to her skin long after it was over. She remembered the offender's face, twisted in a snarl, and the way he seemed to take pleasure in her terror. Even now, when she caught a glimpse of someone with similar features - a sharp jawline or piercing eyes - her breath would catch, and she'd feel like she was back in that alleyway, fighting for her life. As a doctor, Dr. Nguyen had always prided herself on her composure, her ability to stay calm under pressure. But after the assault, she found herself increasingly on edge, jumping at sudden noises or unexpected movements. She began to avoid busy areas of the hospital, opting instead for quieter routes that took her away from potential triggers - like police officers or authority figures who reminded her of the officers who had taken her statement. Even their presence made her feel small and vulnerable all over again. To cope with the anxiety that seemed to claw at her insides, Dr. Nguyen turned to gambling - the rush of adrenaline as she placed a bet, the thrill of possibly winning big. It was a distraction from the memories that haunted her, a way to feel alive when everything else felt numb and gray. She'd conceal herself in baggy clothes, hoping to blend into the background and avoid drawing attention to herself. But even these coping mechanisms brought their own set of problems - she'd lost count of how much money she'd squandered at the casino, and her husband was starting to worry about her increasingly erratic behavior. The smell of antiseptic or freshly laundered scrubs would sometimes transport Dr. Nguyen back to that night, and she'd feel a wave of terror wash over her all over again. It was as if the memory had been seared into her brain, refusing to be extinguished no matter how hard she tried. She couldn't shake the feeling that the world was a fundamentally unsafe place - that strangers lurked around every corner, waiting to pounce. When silence fell, Dr. Nguyen felt like something was off-kilter, like the calm before a storm. It made her skin prickle with unease, and she'd find herself straining to hear any sound that might break the stillness. Loud noises were even worse - they made her jump, her heart racing as if she was back in that alleyway, fighting for survival. Dr. Nguyen had always been a devout person, but after the assault, she found it hard to reconcile her faith with the cruelty of the world. She felt lost and adrift, unable to find solace in the things that used to bring her comfort. Her husband tried to be supportive, but even he couldn't understand why she was so withdrawn, so hesitant to leave the house or engage with the world around her. It wasn't until Dr. Nguyen's supervisor expressed concern about her performance - the mistakes she'd made on the job, the days she'd taken off without explanation - that she realized she needed help. She couldn't keep living like this, trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. As she sat in her therapist's office, pouring out her story for the first time, Dr. Nguyen felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, she could learn to heal, to find a way back to herself. But for now, the memories still lingered, a constant reminder of that terrible night and the terror that had taken up residence in her heart.
